content: White sponge nevus, also referred to as Cannon's disease or hereditary leukokeratosis of mucosa, is a condition that typically follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. While it is congenital in the majority of cases, it may also manifest during childhood or adolescence. The underlying cause of white sponge nevus is a mutation in the keratin 4 (KRT4) and keratin 13 (KRT13) genes. These mutations disrupt the normal function of keratin proteins, which are essential for maintaining the structural integrity of epithelial tissues. Clinically, this condition is characterized by the appearance of thick, white, spongy plaques on the mucosal surfaces of the mouth. These lesions are most commonly bilateral and are frequently observed on the buccal mucosa. Less commonly, they may also involve the labial mucosa, alveolar ridge, or the floor of the mouth. Notably, the gingival margin and the dorsal surface of the tongue are almost never affected. Despite its striking appearance, white sponge nevus is a benign condition and does not pose any significant health risks. However, it is often misdiagnosed as leukoplakia due to its similar clinical presentation. There is no specific treatment for white sponge nevus, as it does not cause any serious clinical complications. The prognosis for individuals with this condition is excellent, and management typically involves reassurance and monitoring. Research has identified specific mutations in the keratin 4 and keratin 13 genes as the molecular basis of this condition. For example, a study by McGowan et al. (2007) described a keratin 4 mutation in a mouse model that mimics white sponge nevus. Similarly, Terrinoni et al. (2001) reported a novel mutation in the keratin 13 gene associated with this disorder. These findings underscore the genetic basis of white sponge nevus and provide insights into its pathophysiology.
